title: SQL Subqueries & Advanced Queries
summary: Covers nested queries, correlated subqueries, EXISTS, IN, ANY, ALL operators, LIKE patterns, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, and BETWEEN.

definitions.definition: A SELECT statement embedded inside another SQL statement. Can appear in WHERE, FROM, or SELECT clauses.
definitions.example: SELECT Name FROM Emp WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Emp);

definitions.definition: A subquery that references columns from the outer query. Executed once for each row of the outer query.
definitions.example: SELECT E.Name FROM Emp E WHERE E.Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Emp WHERE DeptID = E.DeptID);

definitions.definition: Tests if a value matches any value in a list or subquery result. Equivalent to multiple OR conditions.
definitions.example: WHERE DeptID IN (1, 2, 3) same as DeptID=1 OR DeptID=2 OR DeptID=3

definitions.definition: Tests whether a subquery returns any rows. Returns TRUE if subquery has at least one row.
definitions.example: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Orders.CustID = Customers.ID);

definitions.definition: Compares a value to any value returned by a subquery. TRUE if comparison is true for at least one value.
definitions.example: WHERE Salary > ANY (SELECT Salary FROM Emp WHERE Dept='Sales');

definitions.definition: Compares a value to all values returned by a subquery. TRUE only if comparison is true for every value.
definitions.example: WHERE Salary > ALL (SELECT Salary FROM Emp WHERE Dept='Sales');

definitions.definition: Pattern matching operator. % = any sequence of characters. _ = exactly one character.
definitions.example: 't%' matches names starting with t. '%t%' matches names containing t. '_t%' matches t as second character.

definitions.definition: Removes duplicate rows from the result set.
definitions.example: SELECT DISTINCT Dept FROM Employee;

definitions.definition: Sorts query results. ASC (ascending, default) or DESC (descending).
definitions.example: SELECT * FROM Emp ORDER BY Salary DESC;

definitions.definition: Filters values within a range (inclusive).
definitions.example: WHERE Salary BETWEEN 3000 AND 5000;

definitions.definition: The correct operator for removing null values from results. Not IS NONE or LIKE.
definitions.example: WHERE Salary IS NOT NULL;

mustKnowConcepts.title: LIKE Pattern Matching
mustKnowConcepts.description: % = zero or more characters. _ = exactly one character. 't%' = starts with t. '%t' = ends with t. '%t%' = contains t. '_t%' = t is second character.

mustKnowConcepts.title: ORDER BY Default
mustKnowConcepts.description: If ASC or DESC is not specified, ASC (ascending) is the default.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Subquery in WHERE Clause
mustKnowConcepts.description: Most common pattern. The subquery provides a value or set of values for the outer WHERE condition.

mustKnowConcepts.title: IN vs ANY vs ALL
mustKnowConcepts.description: IN: equals any in list. ANY: comparison true for at least one. ALL: comparison true for every value.

mustKnowConcepts.title: IS NOT NULL for Removing NULLs
mustKnowConcepts.description: IS NOT NULL is the correct operator. Not IS NONE, not LIKE, not = NOT NULL.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Multi-column ORDER BY
mustKnowConcepts.description: Can sort by multiple columns: ORDER BY city ASC, assets DESC. First sorts by city, then within each city by assets descending.

examTricks.trick: SELECT * FROM student WHERE name LIKE 't%' — starts with 't'
examTricks.explanation: Not '%t%' (contains t), not '%t' (ends with t), not '_t%' (t as second char). 't%' = starts with t.

examTricks.trick: Default ORDER BY is ASC, not DESC
examTricks.explanation: If you don't specify, results are ascending. This is tested frequently.

examTricks.trick: IN operator tests membership in a list
examTricks.explanation: col IN (v1,v2,v3) is same as col=v1 OR col=v2 OR col=v3. Tests column value against a specified list.

examTricks.trick: IS NOT NULL removes nulls — not IS NONE or = NOT NULL
examTricks.explanation: SQL uses IS NULL / IS NOT NULL syntax. You cannot use = or != with NULL.

examTricks.trick: ANY with subquery: name LIKE pattern uses WHERE, not HAVING
examTricks.explanation: Use WHERE for row-level filtering with LIKE. HAVING is only for aggregate conditions.

confusedConcepts.difference: IN checks if a value is in a set. EXISTS checks if a subquery returns any rows at all.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: IN = is this item on the shopping list? EXISTS = is there any shopping list at all?

confusedConcepts.difference: ANY: true if condition holds for at least one value. ALL: true only if condition holds for every value.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: ANY = at least one friend agrees. ALL = every single friend agrees.

confusedConcepts.difference: % matches zero or more characters (any length). _ matches exactly one character.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: % = elastic band (stretches to any length). _ = one blank space on a form.

keyPoints: IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for nulls

title: Normalization (1NF → BCNF)
summary: Covers functional dependencies, data anomalies, normalization process, and normal forms from 1NF through BCNF. Includes decomposition techniques and identifying violations.

definitions.definition: A constraint X → Y meaning: if two tuples have same X value, they must have same Y value. X determines Y.
definitions.example: SSN → Name (SSN determines Name). StudentID → Name, GPA.

definitions.definition: A relation is in 1NF if: (1) All attribute values are atomic (indivisible), (2) No repeating groups of columns.
definitions.example: A column with 'Math,Science' violates 1NF. Split into separate rows.

definitions.definition: In 1NF AND no partial dependency — every non-key attribute depends on the WHOLE primary key, not just part of it. Only relevant with composite keys.
definitions.example: R(StudentID, CourseID, CourseFee): CourseFee depends only on CourseID (partial dep) → violates 2NF.

definitions.definition: In 2NF AND no transitive dependency — no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute.
definitions.example: If A→B and B→C (both non-key), then A→C is transitive. Remove by decomposing.

definitions.definition: Every determinant (left side of every non-trivial FD) must be a superkey. Stricter than 3NF.
definitions.example: If X→Y and X is not a superkey, the relation violates BCNF.

definitions.definition: A non-key attribute depends on only PART of a composite primary key. Violates 2NF.
definitions.example: Key=(A,B), FD: A→C means C depends on part of key → partial dependency.

definitions.definition: A non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute. If A→B and B→C where B is not a key, then A→C is transitive. Violates 3NF.
definitions.example: StudentID→State, State→Country: StudentID→Country is transitive.

definitions.definition: Problems caused by poor design: Insertion (can't add data without other data), Deletion (losing data when deleting), Modification (inconsistency when updating).
definitions.example: Deleting last employee of a dept loses dept data (deletion anomaly).

definitions.definition: Splitting a relation into smaller relations to achieve a higher normal form while preserving dependencies.
definitions.example: R(A,B,C) with A→B, B→C decomposed to R1(A,B) and R2(B,C) for 3NF.

definitions.definition: An attribute that is part of any candidate key. Non-prime = not part of any candidate key.
definitions.example: If keys are {A,B} and {A,C}, then A, B, C are prime attributes.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Normal Form Hierarchy
mustKnowConcepts.description: 1NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ BCNF. Each higher form is stricter. If a relation fails the n-th NF test, highest NF is (n-1).

mustKnowConcepts.title: Single-Attribute Key → Automatically 2NF
mustKnowConcepts.description: If the primary key has only one attribute, there cannot be partial dependencies, so it's automatically in at least 2NF.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Classic 3NF Violation: A→B, B→C
mustKnowConcepts.description: R(A,B,C) with FDs A→B and B→C where key is A. A→B→C is transitive. R is in 2NF but violates 3NF. Decompose to R1(A,B) and R2(B,C).

mustKnowConcepts.title: Classic 2NF Violation: Partial Dependency
mustKnowConcepts.description: R(X,Y,Z) with key (X,Y) and FD X→Z. Z depends on part of key → partial dependency → violates 2NF.

mustKnowConcepts.title: BCNF: Every Determinant is a Superkey
mustKnowConcepts.description: BCNF is stricter than 3NF. For every FD X→Y, X must be a superkey. 3NF allows non-superkey determinants if Y is prime.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Finding Highest Normal Form
mustKnowConcepts.description: Step 1: Find candidate keys. Step 2: Classify prime vs non-prime attributes. Step 3: Check 1NF→2NF→3NF→BCNF sequentially. Stop at first violation.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Normalization Minimizes Redundancy
mustKnowConcepts.description: The primary goal of normalization is to minimize redundancy, not consistency or fields or integrity.

examTricks.trick: A→B and B→C: this is 2NF but NOT 3NF (transitive dependency)
examTricks.explanation: This is the most frequently tested scenario. The transitive chain violates 3NF.

examTricks.trick: Single-column PK means automatically at least 2NF
examTricks.explanation: No partial dependencies possible with a single-attribute key.

examTricks.trick: If relation fails n-th NF, highest NF = n-1
examTricks.explanation: Example: fails 3NF test → highest normal form is 2NF.

examTricks.trick: ProductID → ProductName in table with composite key (OrderID, ProductID) is a PARTIAL dependency
examTricks.explanation: ProductName depends on ProductID alone, which is only PART of the key. This violates 2NF.

examTricks.trick: 1NF requires atomic values AND no repeating groups
examTricks.explanation: Both conditions must hold. Atomic = no lists/sets in a column. No repeating = no duplicate column groups.

examTricks.trick: Non-key column dependent on another non-key column = transitive dependency
examTricks.explanation: This violates 3NF. The dependency goes through a non-key intermediary.

examTricks.trick: Decomposition for 3NF: R(A,B,C,D) with A,B→C and C→D becomes R1(A,B,C) and R2(C,D)
examTricks.explanation: Split to separate the transitive part. R1 covers AB→C, R2 covers C→D.

examTricks.trick: A relation in 1NF doesn't contain repeating groups, composite attributes as values, or multi-valued attributes in columns
examTricks.explanation: 1NF is about atomicity. No arrays, no sets, no lists in any cell.

confusedConcepts.difference: Partial: non-key depends on PART of composite key (violates 2NF). Transitive: non-key depends on another non-key (violates 3NF).
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Partial = shortcut through part of the key. Transitive = chain through a non-key middleman.

confusedConcepts.difference: 3NF allows non-superkey determinants if the dependent is a prime attribute. BCNF requires ALL determinants to be superkeys.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: 3NF = lenient teacher (allows exceptions). BCNF = strict teacher (no exceptions).

confusedConcepts.difference: Superkey: any set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples. Candidate key: minimal superkey (remove any attribute and it's no longer unique).
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Superkey = any team that can do the job. Candidate key = smallest team that can still do the job.

keyPoints: BCNF: every determinant is a superkey
Partial dep → violates 2NF (only with composite keys)
A→B, B→C: split into R1(A,B) and R2(B,C)

title: Query Processing & Relational Algebra
summary: Covers relational algebra operators (selection σ, projection π, join ⨝, cartesian product ×), query processing steps, query trees, and heuristic query optimization.

definitions.definition: Filters rows/tuples based on a condition. Like WHERE in SQL. σ selects ROWS, not columns.
definitions.example: σ_{Dept='Sales'}(Employee) returns only employees in Sales department.

definitions.definition: Selects specific columns/attributes. Removes other columns. Like SELECT columns in SQL.
definitions.example: π_{Name,Salary}(Employee) returns only Name and Salary columns.

definitions.definition: Combines every row of R with every row of S. 'Meaningless' without a subsequent selection/condition.
definitions.example: If R has 3 rows and S has 4 rows, R × S has 12 rows.

definitions.definition: Combines related tuples from two relations based on a condition. Equivalent to Cartesian product followed by selection.
definitions.example: Employee ⨝_{Dno=Dnumber} Department joins on department number.

definitions.definition: A procedural query language that works on relations to define new relations without changing originals.
definitions.example: σ, π, ×, ⨝, ∪, ∩, − are relational algebra operations.

definitions.definition: A tree representation of a relational algebra expression. Leaves = base relations, internal nodes = RA operations.
definitions.example: Root node might be π (projection), with σ (selection) below, and table leaves at bottom.

definitions.definition: Scanning (lexical analysis), Parsing (syntax check), Validation (semantic check), Optimization, Execution.
definitions.example: Parser checks SQL syntax → Validator checks table/column names exist → Optimizer finds best plan.

definitions.definition: Rules to improve query trees: push selections down, push projections down, replace cartesian+selection with join.
definitions.example: Apply σ early to reduce intermediate result sizes. Move σ close to leaf nodes.

mustKnowConcepts.title: σ (Selection) vs π (Projection)
mustKnowConcepts.description: σ filters ROWS (horizontal). π selects COLUMNS (vertical). σ is like WHERE. π is like SELECT columns. π removes columns, not rows.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Relational Algebra is Procedural
mustKnowConcepts.description: RA is a procedural query language. A language producing relations derivable using RA is relationally complete.

mustKnowConcepts.title: σ_C(R × S) = R ⨝_C S
mustKnowConcepts.description: Selection on a Cartesian product with join condition equals a join. This transformation is a key optimization.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Heuristic: Push Selection Down
mustKnowConcepts.description: Apply σ as early as possible (close to leaves) to reduce the size of intermediate results.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Parser Checks Syntax
mustKnowConcepts.description: In query processing, the parser checks query syntax. Optimizer chooses execution plan. Validator checks semantics.

mustKnowConcepts.title: RA Operations Don't Change Originals
mustKnowConcepts.description: Relational algebra operations work on relations to define new relations WITHOUT changing/storing the original relations.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Projection Removes Columns
mustKnowConcepts.description: π (projection) selects specified columns, discarding others. It removes columns, not rows.

examTricks.trick: σ selects ROWS (tuples), π selects COLUMNS (attributes) — don't mix them up
examTricks.explanation: σ_{Dept='Sales'}(Emp) = rows where Dept is Sales. π_{Name}(Emp) = only the Name column.

examTricks.trick: Cartesian product is 'meaningless' without a subsequent selection
examTricks.explanation: R × S gives every pair. You need σ or a join condition to make it useful.

examTricks.trick: Relational algebra is PROCEDURAL query language
examTricks.explanation: Not DDL, not meta language, not non-procedural. RA is procedural.
π removes columns. It does NOT remove rows, NULL values, or duplicate rows (well, it removes duplicate rows in formal RA).

examTricks.trick: Query optimization minimizes execution COST (I/O, CPU), not number of tables or result size
examTricks.explanation: The goal is to minimize resource usage, not minimize output.

examTricks.trick: SQL to RA conversion: σ corresponds to WHERE, π corresponds to SELECT columns
examTricks.explanation: SELECT Name FROM Emp WHERE Dept='Sales' = π_{Name}(σ_{Dept='Sales'}(Employee))

confusedConcepts.difference: σ filters rows (horizontal slice, like WHERE). π selects columns (vertical slice, like SELECT columns).
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: σ = slicing cake horizontally (layers/rows). π = slicing vertically (columns/portions).

confusedConcepts.difference: × gives ALL combinations (no condition). ⨝ gives only matching combinations (with condition). ⨝ = × followed by σ.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: × = mixing all ingredients randomly. ⨝ = combining only ingredients that go together.

confusedConcepts.difference: Procedural (RA): specify HOW to get results step by step. Non-procedural (SQL/Calculus): specify WHAT you want, system decides how.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Procedural = giving GPS turn-by-turn directions. Non-procedural = telling GPS the destination.
